Densities (i.e. averaged over all cortical layers) of each of the 14 different receptors in 33 of the 35 cytoarchitectonically defined areas were calculated. Due to technical limitations associated with the cutting angle of the coronal sections, it was not possible to measure densities in areas 13a and 14c. The precise sampling for the measurements of each cytoarchitectonically defined area was verified by aligning autoradiographs with defined cytoarchitectonic borders in neighbouring silver-staining sections in the corresponding brain processed for the receptor architectonic analysis. For each of the examined areas and their subdivisions, the mean densities of all receptors averaged over all four hemispheres in that area were then visualized simultaneously as ‘receptor fingerprints,’ that is, as polar coordinate plots which reveal the specific balance of different receptor types within a cytoarchitectonic entity (Zilles et al., 2002). #### Statistical analysis of the receptor densities To determine whether there were significant differences in receptor architecture between paired areas (in particular our analysis was focused on directly bordering areas within the prefrontal region), stepwise linear mixed-effect models were performed. A z-score normalization was performed for each receptor separately to ensure an equal weighting of all receptors in subsequent statistical analyses. All statistical analyses were conducted using the R programming language (version 3.6.3.; Team, 2013). We conducted a statistical testing which included three levels. In the first level, an omnibus test was carried out to determine whether there were differences across all regions when all receptor types are considered simultaneously (Equation 2). The model consists of fixed effects for area and receptor type, and hemisphere was set as a random factor. $$ D_{a,r,h}=\alpha_{o}+\alpha_{1}A_{a}+\alpha_{2}R_{r}+\alpha_{3}A_{a}R_{r}+\beta_{1}H_{h} $$ where D represents the receptor density, A is the prefrontal area, R is the receptor type, and H is the hemisphere. If the interaction effect between area and receptor type at first level of testing was found to be significant, a second level of simple effect tests was applied for each receptor separately to determine whether there were significant differences across all areas for each receptor type. The p-values were corrected for multiple comparison using the Benjamini–Hochberg correction for false discovery rate (Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995). Finally, the third-level post hoc tests were used to identify the paired areas driving the statistical difference in the second-level tests. For each receptor type, 528 post hoc tests were performed. To correct for multiple comparisons in the third step tests, we performed the false discovery rate correction (Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995) separately for each receptor type (i.e. p-values were corrected for 528 comparisons per receptor type). ### Visualization and analysis of functional connectivity All datasets used here for analysis are openly available sources from the recently established PRIME-DE (http://fcon_1000.projects.nitrc.org/indi/indiPRIME.html; Milham et al., 2018). Resting-state fMRI data from 19 macaque monkeys (all males, age = 4.01 ± 0.98 y) was collected with no contrast agent on a 3T scanner with a four-channel coil in Oxford (Noonan et al., 2014). For each animal, one resting-state scan (6.67 min, 250 volumes) was used. These data were downloaded from the PRIME-DE database (Milham et al., 2018) and preprocessed using a Human Connectome Project-like pipeline for Nonhuman Primate as described previously (Autio et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2019). For each macaque, the structural preprocessing includes denoising, skull-stripping, tissue segmentation, surface reconstruction, and surface registration to align to Yerkes19 macaque surface template (Donahue et al., 2016). The functional preprocessing includes temporal compressing, motion, correction, global mean scaling, nuisance regression (Friston’s 24 motion parameters, white matter, cerebrospinal fluid), band-pass filtering (0.01–0.1 Hz), and linear and quadratic detrending. The preprocessed data then were co-registered to the anatomy T1 and projected to the middle cortical surface. Finally, the data were smoothed (FWHM = 3 mm) on the high-resolution native surface, aligned, and downresampled to a 10k surface (10,242 vertices per hemisphere). The preprocessed BOLD activity time courses for each monkey brain were demeaned and then concatenated in time. This enabled us to estimate the group functional connectivity maps for each seed region in a single analysis. The connectivity of each identified prefrontal areas was investigated in regard to 76 cortical areas, previously defined by Palomero-Gallagher group, that is, 16 areas of (pre)motor cortex, 15 areas of cingulate cortex, 6 areas of somatosensory cortex, 23 areas of parietal cortex, and 16 areas of occipital cortex (Impieri et al., 2019; Niu et al., 2021; Rapan et al., 2021; Rapan et al., 2022). A representative time course was calculated for each of the 35 prefrontal areas and the 76 (pre)motor, cingulate, somatosensory, parietal, and occipital areas, giving 111 areas in total. For each of the 111 areas, a principal components analysis was performed on activity across all vertices within the area, where the first principal component was taken as the representative activity time course for each area. The representative time courses of each of the 35 prefrontal areas were used as seeds for functional connectivity analysis. Since they were correlated with the activity time courses for each vertex on the surface using a Pearson correlation. A Fisher’s r-to-z transformation was then applied to each of the correlation coefficients. This was visualized on the Yerkes19 cortical surface. Code used for the implementation and visualization of the functional connectivity analysis has been made publicly available (https://github.com/seanfw/macaque-pfc-func-conn, copy archived at Rapan, 2023). ### Multivariate analyses of receptor fingerprints To reveal structure–function relationship between areas of the frontal lobe, we not only used receptor fingerprints of the here identified 33 prefrontal areas (except areas 13a and 14c, see above), but also included those of previously identified 16 motor and premotor areas (Rapan et al., 2021). Receptor densities were extracted from the same macaque brains. Hierarchical clustering and principal component analyses were carried out to enable grouping of areas based on receptor architectonic similarities (Palomero-Gallagher et al., 2009). We used a receptor fingerprint of each area as a feature vector characterizing the area of interest. The Euclidean distance, which takes into account difference in the size and shape of fingerprint, was applied as a measure of (dis)similarities between receptor fingerprints. Before any statistical analysis was conducted, it was necessary to normalize all absolute receptor values due to large differences in absolute densities across receptor types. Receptors with high absolute density values (i.e. GABAergic receptors) would dominate the calculation of the Euclidean distance between areas, as well as of the principal component analysis, cancelling intended multimodal approach in the present analysis. Whereas normalized receptor values enable for each receptor type to contribute with equal significance to the statistical analyses. Here, z-scores calculation was applied since this approach maintains the relative differences in receptor densities among areas, that is, the mean density of a given receptor across all examined areas was subtracted from the mean density of the same receptor in a defined area and obtained value was divided by the standard deviation of that receptor over all areas. The Ward linkage algorithm was chosen as the linkage method in combination with the Euclidean distances. It yielded a higher cophenetic correlation coefficient than any other combination of alternative linkage methods and measurements of (dis)similarity. The cophenetic correlation coefficient quantifies how well the dendrogram represents the true, multidimensional distances within the input data. The k-means analysis was applied to identify the highest acceptable number of clusters and confirmed by the k-means permutation test.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "Cytoarchitectonic, receptor distribution and functional connectivity analyses of the macaque frontal lobe" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by 3 peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor, David Badre, and Chris Baker as the Senior Editor. The following individual involved in the review of your submission has agreed to reveal their identity: Michel Thiebaut de Schotten (Reviewer #3).

The Reviewers were universally positive about the contribution and quality of these findings. However, they did have some points of revision that can help improve the clarity and the impact of the work. I refer you to the specific comments from the reviewers below for details. However, their comments highlight some essential revisions.

1) Reviewer 1 raises the point that connectivity to the temporal lobe is important to include in your analysis of the prefrontal cortex.

2) Reviewer 2 points out that the relationship to the Walker map could be made clearer.

3) All three reviewers highlighted several points to be clarified and tightened both in the introduction and discussion, as well as clarifying some aspects of the design and methods.

Reviewer #1 (Recommendations for the authors):

The design of the study is not completely clear. Indeed, the reason for analyzing prefrontal and frontal areas together in the cluster analysis is not explained. In the introduction, the authors state that quantification of heterogeneous receptor distribution throughout the cerebral cortex enables the identification of subdivisions among primary sensory, primary motor, and multimodal areas. However, they analyzed prefrontal data only with those of caudal frontal areas. The authors have also, from previous studies, receptor density data of parietal and cingulate areas, thus they could have also included these areas in the cluster analysis. Furthermore, in the introduction, the authors said that functional connectivity data could "resonate" with those of receptor density, but most of the analyzed receptors reflect the presence of subcortical input, not cortical connectivity. Finally, in the discussion, the results of cluster analysis are interpreted in a way that is not supported by their data ("functional clustering", e.g., oculomotor interpretation of the entire cluster 4).

The introduction could be more focused. Specifically, the issue of homologies between macaque and human cortical areas is introduced but then not addressed, as well as the issue of variability of parcellations. Furthermore, the authors introduce the issue of variability between brains, but from the methods, I understand that the observer-independent cytoarchitectonic analysis was performed on only one subject (DP1) and that the other brains are then qualitatively subdivided as brain DP1.

The number and dimension of the samples analyzed for autoradiography in each brain for each area are not clear. Accordingly, the assessment of variability between samples and brains is not clear. In the observer-independent cytoarchitectonic analysis, the concept of ROIs is not well defined.

The authors excluded parts of areas 14 (14c) and 13 (13a) because of the plane of cut. What about area 8 within the most posterior part of the inferior arcuate sulcus?

I suggest using "area" and "subdivision" more consistently within the text.

Reviewer #2 (Recommendations for the authors):

In this impressive study, Rapan and colleagues did perform a multi-modal parcellation of the macaque frontal cortex based on cytoarchitectonic, receptor architecture data in fascicularis macaques and resting-state functional fMRI data in anaesthetized rhesus macaques.

Compared with the classic Walker map of the macaque frontal cortex, the authors produced a more refined map.

Some areas they identified had been already reported in previous studies and atlases (Petrides et al. 2012 Cortex; Reveley et al. 2017 Cerebral Cortex; Saleem and Logothetis 2012), although arguably with different names. How does the proposed parcellation fit with previous ones? More specifically how do the authors consider areas 9/46d and 9/46v?

How does the clustering based on receptor fingerprints correlate with a clustering based on functional connectivity fingerprints (see also Goulas et al. 2017 J. Neurophysiology)? Clusters based on receptors densities appear to be distinct from published connectivity parcellation (Goulas et al. 2017 J. Neurophysiology; Giarracco and Averbeck 2021 J. Neurophysiology; Hutchinson and Everling 2014 Neuroimage). results.result: The study identified 35 prefrontal areas using quantitative cyto- and receptor architectonic analyses, including novel subdivisions of Walker's areas 10, 9, 8B, and 46. The systematic identification resulted in a map showing the location and extent of all areas and their relationships with macroanatomical landmarks.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C28, and C29 collectively describe the primary outcome of the cytoarchitectonic analysis. The identification of 35 areas is explicitly stated in the abstract and results, with detailed documentation in figures and tables showing the spatial relationships and comparisons with previous maps. The quantitative methods and statistical validation provide robust support for these findings.

results.result: Statistical analysis revealed regional differences in receptor densities in lateral and ventrolateral prefrontal cortex, with significant differences in α2 receptor levels between subdivisions of areas 46 and 12. The structural and functional organization of these subdivisions appears closely related to differences in interareal α2 receptor levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C3, C38, C39, and C40 describe significant receptor density differences with statistical support (Table 4). The finding that medially positioned areas (12m, 12o) have significantly higher α2 receptor densities than lateral areas (12r, 12l) is explicitly stated with statistical validation. The inference about structure-function relationships (C40) is reasonable given the convergent evidence from receptor architecture and functional connectivity.

results.result: Multivariate analysis of receptor fingerprints from 33 prefrontal areas and 16 motor areas revealed 5 clusters encompassing frontal lobe areas. The hierarchical cluster analysis showed differences in receptor fingerprint size between rostral and caudal areas, with principal component analysis revealing a rostro-caudal trend driven by gradual decrease in receptor fingerprint size.
results.evaluation: Claims C4 and C55-C61 describe the multivariate analysis results with clear documentation in Figures 19 and 20. The identification of 5 clusters using k-means analysis is explicitly stated, and the rostro-caudal gradient in receptor density is well-documented. The principal component analysis results are clearly presented, showing segregation of different functional regions. The analysis appropriately uses normalized receptor densities to avoid bias from high-density receptors.

results.result: Rostrally located frontal areas were characterized by larger receptor fingerprints (higher receptor densities) and stronger regional interconnections, whereas more caudal areas had smaller fingerprints but showed widespread connectivity patterns with distant cortical regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C5 and C6 summarize the rostro-caudal organizational principle revealed by the combined receptor and functional connectivity analyses. The receptor density data (Table 3, Figures 10-11) clearly show higher densities in rostral areas, and the functional connectivity analyses (Figures 12-18) demonstrate the differential connectivity patterns. This represents a well-supported integration of structural and functional findings.

results.result: The frontopolar region (areas 10) is characterized by the highest density of kainate and GABAA/BZ receptors among all prefrontal areas examined. Changes in laminar patterns of GABAA, M1, M2, α1, and 5HT1A receptors highlight cytoarchitectonically defined borders within area 10, with dorsoventral subdivisions showing differences in fingerprint size.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C35 describe the receptor architecture of area 10 with explicit reference to Table 3 and figures. The highest densities of kainate and GABAA/BZ receptors in area 10 are documented in Table 3. Significant differences between subdivisions and adjacent areas are statistically validated (Table 4). The laminar patterns are shown in Figure 9 and supplements, providing visual confirmation of the borders.

results.result: Medial frontopolar areas 10md and 10mv showed strong functional connectivity with cingulate cortex (areas p32 and s32), which have established homologies in the human brain associated with emotion processing.
results.evaluation: Claim C36 presents functional connectivity data from the study's analysis, while C37 cites established literature (Palomero-Gallagher et al., 2013, 2019; Vogt et al., 2013) supporting the homology and functional associations. The connectivity patterns are documented in Figure 12, and the interpretation is appropriately grounded in cited literature. This represents a valid integration of current findings with established knowledge.

results.result: Areas 9d and 9l show significantly higher receptor densities than their caudal counterparts in area 8B for multiple receptor types. Area 8Av was characterized by the lowest density of multiple receptor types (AMPA, GABAB, M1, M3, α1, α2, 5HT1A) among all prefrontal areas analyzed.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C46 describe significant receptor density differences between areas 9 and 8B, and the unique characteristics of area 8Av. These findings are explicitly stated with statistical support (Table 4) and documented in Table 3 and Figures 11. The identification of area 8Av as having the smallest receptor fingerprint in the PFC is clearly supported by the data.

results.result: Within area 46, higher receptor densities were found in areas around the fundus of the principal sulcus than on its dorsal and ventral shoulders. Significantly higher α2 receptor densities were found in fundal areas along the entire length of the principal sulcus, and higher muscarinic cholinergic densities were found in anterior subdivisions compared to posterior counterparts.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C50 describe the detailed receptor architecture of area 46 subdivisions with explicit reference to Tables 3 and 4. The rostro-caudal and dorso-ventral gradients in receptor densities are well-documented. The significant differences in α2 receptors between fundal and shoulder areas are statistically validated. This fine-grained parcellation of area 46 represents a novel contribution supported by convergent cyto- and receptor architectonic evidence.

results.result: Area 45A contains significantly higher kainate levels than 45B. Area 44 had the highest concentration of 5HT2 receptors and one of the highest 5-HT1A receptor densities within the PFC, while area 45A contains the second lowest PFC density of 5-HT1A receptors.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C54 describe receptor differences in ventrolateral prefrontal areas with explicit reference to Tables 3 and 4. The significant difference in kainate between 45A and 45B is statistically validated (Table 4). The unique receptor profile of area 44, particularly for serotonergic receptors, is clearly documented in Table 3 and Figure 11, supporting its distinct functional role.

results.result: The study aimed to identify and characterize prefrontal areas using quantitative cyto- and receptor architectonic approaches and create a 3D statistically validated parcellation scheme in stereotaxic space. Receptor fingerprints of premotor areas were obtained from the same brains as prefrontal areas, and all data are made available via EBRAINS and BALSA repositories.
results.evaluation: Claims C23, C26, and C27 describe the study's aims and methodological approach. The primary aim is explicitly stated in the introduction, the use of the same brains for both prefrontal and motor areas is confirmed, and data availability is stated in both the introduction and methods. This represents appropriate transparency and data sharing practices.

results.result: Functional connectivity analysis revealed tight coupling between posterior prefrontal and premotor areas, which was hypothesized to be associated with similarities in neurochemical composition.
results.evaluation: Claim C24 presents functional connectivity findings, while C25 states the hypothesis that motivated including motor areas in the multivariate analysis. The functional connectivity results (Figures 13-18) demonstrate the tight coupling, and the multivariate analysis (Figure 19) shows that some posterior prefrontal areas cluster with premotor areas, supporting the hypothesis. The hypothesis is appropriately presented as such and is tested by the subsequent analyses.

results.result: The medial OFC is associated with value comparison and motivation in decision-making, while the lateral OFC is involved in reward-associated behavior by assigning value to stimuli. Specific areas (14r, 14c, 13a, 11m, 12o) serve as intermediary areas connecting lateral and medial OFC networks.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C66 integrate the current study's findings with established literature on OFC function. The claims appropriately cite supporting studies (Price, 2007; Carmichael and Price, 1994; Noonan et al., 2010; Rudebeck and Murray, 2011b) and relate them to the identified subdivisions. The functional interpretations are grounded in cited lesion and connectivity studies, providing appropriate context for the current anatomical findings.

results.result: Microstimulation recordings revealed auditory-responsive neurons within the caudal principal sulcus, though most auditory cortex input targets the rostral portion and frontopolar region. PFC areas grouped in cluster 1 based on receptor fingerprint similarities appear involved in distinct aspects of reward-guided behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C68 cite established literature (Hackett et al., 1999; Ito, 1982; Watanabe, 1992; Barbas and Mesulam, 1985; Medalla and Barbas, 2014) documenting auditory inputs to prefrontal areas. Claim C69 infers functional involvement from the clustering analysis and literature, which is reasonable given that cluster 1 includes orbitofrontal and frontopolar areas known to be involved in reward processing. The inference is appropriately qualified as 'seem to be involved.'

results.result: Area F5v is associated with mouth movements and feeding-related behavior, sharing connections with gustatory, orbitofrontal, insular, and somatosensory cortex. Areas of posterior orbital PFC represent a multimodal region targeted by multiple sensory cortices and the amygdala. Area 9l may serve as a bridge between multimodal lateral PFC and polysensory posterior orbital cortex.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C72 appropriately cite supporting literature (Maranesi et al., 2012; Cipolloni and Pandya, 1999; Barbas, 2007) for functional associations and connectivity patterns. The speculation is appropriately qualified with 'may be' and is grounded in the observed connectivity data.

results.evaluation: Claims C74 and C75 cite an electrophysiology study (Lanzilotto et al., 2017) and relate it to the identified areas 9l and 9d. The topological correspondence between the recorded region and the identified areas is reasonable given the anatomical descriptions. The functional interpretation is appropriately attributed to the cited study, and the inference about social function is grounded in the mirror neuron findings.

results.result: Medial area F6 plays an important role in controlling complex motor plans but lacks direct connections to primary motor areas and spinal cord, mediating its contribution to movement via dense connections with other premotor areas. The correlation between F6 and primary motor area 4m may reflect indirect rather than direct connections.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C79 appropriately cite supporting literature (Matelli et al., 1991; Dum and Strick, 2002; Luppino et al., 1993; Adachi et al., 2012) for F6's function and connectivity. results.result: Area F3 contains a complete somatotopic map with direct connections to primary motor cortex. Area 8B is a target of prestriate and medial parietal cortex, constitutes the cytoarchitectonic correlate of PEEF involved in auditory stimuli recognition and orientation, and is thought to be monkey-specific with no human homolog due to its role in integrating auditory inputs with ear and eye motor output.

The hypothesis that area 8B is monkey-specific (C85) is appropriately qualified as 'thought to be' and is grounded in the functional differences between monkeys and humans in ear movement for sound localization (C86).

Areas 8Bd and F7d are associated with SEF, while area 8Ad is partly associated with FEF. SEF and FEF differ in that FEF saccades are of fixed vectors while SEF represents eye position.

The inference about transitional status is reasonable given the convergent cytoarchitectonic, receptor architectonic, and functional connectivity evidence.

results.result: The prefrontal cortex is involved in higher cognitive functions. Macaque monkeys are the most widely used primate species in neurobiological research, share a similar basic architectonic plan to humans, and are important for research due to ethical limitations on human brain studies. Walker's 1940 parcellation scheme became the basis for future studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C13 provide background context with appropriate citations (Fuster, 2008; DeFelipe, 2015; Passingham, 2009; Petrides et al., 2012; Petrides and Pandya, 1994, 1999, 2002, 2009; Walker, 1940; Brodmann, 1905, 1909; Barbas and Pandya, 1989; Carmichael and Price, 1996; Morecraft et al., 2012; Petrides and Pandya, 2006). These are well-established facts in the field and provide appropriate context for the study.

results.result: Quantitative in vitro multireceptor autoradiography is a powerful tool for describing brain molecular and functional organization. Receptor concentrations vary between cortical areas, and the area-specific balance of receptor types (receptor fingerprint) subserves distinct functional properties. Multivariate analyses of receptor fingerprints demonstrate structurally and functionally significant clustering of cortical areas.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C18 provide methodological background with appropriate citations (Impieri et al., 2019; Palomero-Gallagher et al., 2009; Zilles et al., 2002; Palomero-Gallagher and Zilles, 2019; Zilles and Palomero-Gallagher, 2017b; Zilles and Amunts, 2009). These represent established principles in the field and provide appropriate justification for the methodological approach used in the study.

results.result: In vivo neuroimaging of non-human primates has been advancing rapidly, but integration with postmortem anatomical data has been problematic due to lack of common coordinate space. Several digital macaque atlases have been created, but currently available maps do not contain receptor density information.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C22 provide context for the study's contribution with appropriate citations (Milham et al., 2018, 2020; Bezgin et al., 2012; Frey et al., 2011; McLaren et al., 2009; Moirano et al., 2019; Reveley et al., 2017; Van Essen et al., 2012). These claims establish the gap in existing knowledge that the current study addresses, particularly the lack of receptor density information in available atlases.
